questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Dengue virus has how many distinct serotypes?
questions.concept: DENV-1 to DENV-4 give lifelong homotypic immunity but only transient cross-protection, so a person can have four infections. Secondary infection with a different serotype carries the highest risk of severe dengue.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Antibody-dependent enhancement explains why:
options: Secondary infection with a different dengue serotype is more severe than primary infection
questions.concept: Non-neutralising cross-reactive antibodies bind the new serotype and facilitate Fc receptor-mediated uptake into monocytes, amplifying viral load and cytokine release with plasma leakage - the basis of dengue vaccine safety concerns.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: NS1 antigen testing for dengue is most useful:
options: In the first five days of illness, before IgM appears
questions.concept: NS1 is detectable from day 1 to about day 5 of fever, filling the diagnostic gap before IgM becomes positive around day 5, so NS1 and IgM together cover the whole illness.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Japanese encephalitis is maintained in nature by a cycle involving:
options: Pigs as amplifying hosts and ardeid birds as reservoirs, with Culex vectors
questions.concept: Humans are dead-end hosts with low viraemia, so control targets vector reduction, pig management away from dwellings and vaccination in endemic districts. Culex tritaeniorhynchus breeds in rice fields.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Zika virus infection is of greatest concern because of:
questions.concept: Zika is usually mild but is neurotropic and teratogenic, causing congenital Zika syndrome with microcephaly and brain calcification. Unusually for an arbovirus, it is also sexually and vertically transmitted.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: The tourniquet (Hess) test in dengue assesses:
options: Capillary fragility, becoming positive with 10 or more petechiae per square inch
questions.concept: Inflating a cuff to midway between systolic and diastolic pressure for five minutes and counting petechiae in a 2.5 cm square gives a simple bedside indicator of capillary fragility, though it is neither sensitive nor specific.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: The mainstay of dengue management is:
options: Careful isotonic crystalloid fluid therapy guided by haematocrit and vital signs
questions.concept: There is no specific antiviral; judicious fluid replacement during the critical phase of plasma leakage prevents shock, while excess fluid causes overload. Platelets are transfused only for significant bleeding, not for a low count alone.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Aedes aegypti control is difficult in urban India because the mosquito:
options: Breeds in small clean water collections in and around houses and bites during the day
questions.concept: Domestic breeding in coolers, tyres, tanks and flowerpots means control depends on community-based source reduction rather than spraying alone, and daytime biting makes bed nets largely ineffective.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Japanese encephalitis vaccine in the Indian programme is given:
options: As a live attenuated vaccine in endemic districts at 9 months with a booster at 16 to 24 months
questions.concept: The live attenuated SA 14-14-2 vaccine has been incorporated into routine immunisation in endemic districts, along with campaign-mode catch-up vaccination, and has substantially reduced incidence.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Chikungunya differs from dengue clinically by causing:
options: Severe persistent symmetrical polyarthralgia lasting weeks to months
questions.concept: Both are transmitted by Aedes with overlapping acute features, but chikungunya causes disabling arthralgia that may persist for months, while dengue causes plasma leakage, shock and haemorrhage.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Blood cultures for suspected bacteraemia should ideally be collected:
options: Before starting antibiotics, from two or three separate sites
questions.concept: Prior antibiotics markedly reduce yield, and multiple sets from separate venepunctures distinguish true bacteraemia from skin contaminants. Adequate blood volume is the single most important determinant of sensitivity.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: In suspected enteric fever, the specimen with the highest yield in the first week of illness is:
questions.concept: Blood culture is positive in about 80% in week one, stool and urine cultures become positive in the second and third weeks, and bone marrow culture has the highest yield overall and remains positive despite antibiotics.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: The main limitation of the Widal test is that:
options: Titres are affected by prior infection and vaccination, and a single titre is not diagnostic
questions.concept: A four-fold rise in paired sera is needed for meaningful interpretation, and endemic background titres, previous typhoid, vaccination and anamnestic responses cause false positives; early antibiotics blunt the response.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Cerebrospinal fluid for suspected bacterial meningitis must be:
options: Transported immediately at room temperature and never refrigerated
questions.concept: Meningococcus and Haemophilus are highly susceptible to cold and drying, so refrigeration kills them. CSF is processed urgently with Gram stain, cell count, biochemistry and culture, plus latex agglutination or PCR.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Sputum is considered an acceptable specimen for culture when microscopy shows:
options: More than 25 neutrophils and fewer than 10 squamous epithelial cells per low-power field
questions.concept: Abundant squamous cells indicate salivary contamination, making culture uninterpretable. Screening by these Bartlett or Murray-Washington criteria avoids reporting misleading oropharyngeal flora.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification testing (CBNAAT/GeneXpert) for tuberculosis provides:
options: Detection of M. tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance within about two hours
questions.concept: Xpert MTB/RIF is far more sensitive than smear microscopy, detects rpoB mutations conferring rifampicin resistance simultaneously, and is now the recommended initial diagnostic test under the national programme.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A four-fold rise in antibody titre between acute and convalescent sera indicates:
questions.concept: Paired sera taken 10 to 14 days apart showing a four-fold rise is the classical serological criterion for recent infection, overcoming the problem of interpreting a single titre against unknown background exposure.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Polymerase chain reaction is particularly valuable for organisms that:
options: Are difficult or hazardous to culture, or when the patient has received antibiotics
questions.concept: PCR detects nucleic acid regardless of viability, making it useful for fastidious organisms such as Mycobacterium, Chlamydia, Bordetella and viruses, though it cannot distinguish live from dead organisms and risks contamination.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Urine for culture should be a:
options: Clean-catch midstream sample processed within two hours or refrigerated
Sample from the bag of a catheter
questions.concept: Delay allows contaminant multiplication producing falsely high counts. Significant bacteriuria is conventionally 10 to the power 5 organisms per mL, though lower counts matter in symptomatic women and suprapubic aspirates.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Transport medium is used for specimens to:
options: Preserve organism viability without allowing overgrowth during transit
questions.concept: Stuart, Amies and Cary-Blair media are semi-solid, nutrient-poor and buffered, keeping delicate organisms alive without letting hardy commensals multiply and swamp the pathogen.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Cornea: keratitis, ulcers, dystrophies & corneal transplant
questions.stem: A dendritic corneal ulcer staining with fluorescein indicates:
questions.concept: The branching dendrite with terminal bulbs is characteristic of herpes simplex epithelial keratitis, treated with topical acyclovir. Topical steroids alone are contraindicated as they cause a geographic ulcer.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Cornea: keratitis, ulcers, dystrophies & corneal transplant
questions.stem: A corneal ulcer with feathery margins and satellite lesions in a farmer after injury with vegetative matter suggests:
questions.concept: Fusarium and Aspergillus keratitis follows vegetative trauma, showing dry raised ulcers with feathery edges, satellite lesions and an immune ring. Natamycin is first line; steroids are strictly contraindicated.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Cornea: keratitis, ulcers, dystrophies & corneal transplant
questions.stem: Severe pain out of proportion to signs with a ring infiltrate in a contact lens wearer suggests:
questions.concept: Acanthamoeba is associated with contact lens use and exposure to contaminated water, causing disproportionate pain, radial keratoneuritis and a ring infiltrate. Diagnosis is by confocal microscopy or culture on non-nutrient agar with E. coli.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Cornea: keratitis, ulcers, dystrophies & corneal transplant
questions.stem: Hypopyon in a corneal ulcer represents:
options: Sterile inflammatory exudate settling in the anterior chamber
questions.concept: Hypopyon in bacterial keratitis is usually sterile, resulting from toxin-driven inflammation with an intact Descemet membrane, so intraocular tap is not routinely needed. It indicates severe disease requiring intensive therapy.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Cornea: keratitis, ulcers, dystrophies & corneal transplant
questions.stem: Keratoconus is characterised by:
options: Progressive corneal thinning and conical protrusion with irregular astigmatism
questions.concept: Keratoconus presents in adolescence with progressive myopic astigmatism, Munson sign, Fleischer ring and Vogt striae. Rigid contact lenses, corneal collagen cross-linking to halt progression and keratoplasty are the treatment options.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Cornea: keratitis, ulcers, dystrophies & corneal transplant
questions.stem: The commonest indication for penetrating keratoplasty in India is:
questions.concept: Post-infectious corneal opacity, largely preventable, remains the leading indication in India, whereas Fuchs dystrophy and pseudophakic bullous keratopathy dominate in developed countries.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Cornea: keratitis, ulcers, dystrophies & corneal transplant
questions.stem: Corneal grafts enjoy relatively high success because the cornea is:
questions.concept: Avascularity and absent lymphatics limit antigen presentation, giving immune privilege. Vascularisation from previous inflammation is the main risk factor for graft rejection, indicated by the Khodadoust line.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Cornea: keratitis, ulcers, dystrophies & corneal transplant
questions.stem: A Kayser-Fleischer ring is deposition of copper in:
options: Descemet membrane at the corneal periphery
questions.concept: Copper deposits in Descemet membrane produce a golden-brown peripheral ring best seen on gonioscopy, and is a diagnostic feature of Wilson disease, often accompanied by a sunflower cataract.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Cornea: keratitis, ulcers, dystrophies & corneal transplant
questions.stem: Vitamin A deficiency causing corneal melting and perforation is termed:
questions.concept: Keratomalacia is the end stage of xerophthalmia, a blinding emergency in malnourished children requiring immediate high-dose vitamin A. The sequence runs night blindness, conjunctival xerosis, Bitot spots, corneal xerosis, ulceration then keratomalacia.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Cornea: keratitis, ulcers, dystrophies & corneal transplant
questions.stem: Topical corticosteroids in a red eye are dangerous because they can:
options: Worsen herpetic and fungal keratitis, raise intraocular pressure and cause cataract
questions.concept: Steroid use without slit-lamp examination and fluorescein staining risks corneal melt, perforation and blindness, in addition to steroid-induced glaucoma and posterior subcapsular cataract with prolonged use.
